questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a multinational corporation?
options: A business that owns or controls production or service operations in more than one country
A business that exports to more than one country
A business owned by shareholders from several countries
A business listed on more than one stock exchange
questions.why: Ownership or control of operations abroad is what makes a business multinational, not simply selling abroad.
whyNot: That is an exporter.
Shareholder nationality does not determine multinational status.
A multiple listing is a financing arrangement.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines profit repatriation?
options: The transfer of profits earned in a host country back to the multinational's home country
The reinvestment of profits in the host country
The payment of tax on profits in the host country
The distribution of profits to local employees
questions.why: Repatriated profit is a debit on the host country's primary income account every year.
whyNot: That is reinvestment, which has the opposite effect.
That is taxation.
That is profit sharing.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines transfer pricing?
options: Setting the prices at which parts of the same multinational trade with each other
Charging different prices in different countries
Transferring ownership of a business to a local partner
The price paid to acquire a foreign company
questions.why: It can be used to move reported profit to low-tax countries, which is the sharpest criticism of the tax benefit MNCs bring.
whyNot: That is price discrimination.
That is a divestment.
That is the acquisition price.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines crowding out in this context?
options: A large entrant taking customers, staff or suppliers from local businesses
Government borrowing raising interest rates for private firms
Overcrowding of a local labour market by migrant workers
Too many products competing for shelf space
questions.why: Local competitors may be unable to match a multinational's prices, marketing or purchasing power.
whyNot: That is the macroeconomic meaning of the term, used in Economics.
That is labour market pressure, a different effect.
That is a retail issue.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a local benefit of an MNC's arrival?
options: Employment at wages often above the local average, with training and transferable skills
The elimination of all local competition, which benefits consumers
A guaranteed permanent rise in national wages
The removal of the need for local suppliers
questions.why: An indirect employment multiplier also arises as local suppliers and services grow around the operation.
whyNot: Eliminating competition harms consumers in the long run.
Wage effects are real but not guaranteed or economy-wide.
Local sourcing is one of the main potential benefits.

questions.stem: Why is it said that paying above the local average and below the home rate are both true?
options: Which comparison the answer uses determines the conclusion, so a good answer says so explicitly
Wage data is always unreliable
Multinationals pay the same wage in every country
Local averages exclude multinational employers
questions.why: Naming the choice of comparison is the examinable nuance in this part of the topic.
whyNot: Wage comparisons are imperfect but usable.
They pay very different wages in different countries.
Local averages include all employers.

questions.stem: How does the initial FDI appear in the host country's balance of payments?
options: As an inflow on the financial account
As a debit on the current account
As a credit on the primary income account
It does not appear at all
questions.why: Exports produced by the operation are current account credits, while imported inputs and repatriated profit are debits.
whyNot: The investment itself is a financial account inflow.
Repatriated profit, not the investment, affects primary income.
It is recorded in the financial account.

questions.stem: Why can the balance of payments effect of FDI turn negative over time?
options: Repatriated profit is an annual outflow that can eventually exceed the original investment
Exports from the operation fall to zero after a few years
The initial investment must be repaid to the investor
Host countries must pay interest on inward FDI
questions.why: The effect is positive at first and can become permanently negative once cumulative repatriation exceeds the inflow.
whyNot: Exports usually continue.
Equity investment is not repaid like a loan.
FDI is equity, not debt, so no interest is due.

questions.stem: Which of the following limits technology and skills transfer?
options: The most valuable research and development usually stays in the home country
Host countries prohibit the transfer of technology
Technology cannot be moved across borders
Workers refuse to be trained
questions.why: Transfer also requires local firms and workers capable of absorbing it, which depends on the education system.
whyNot: Most host countries actively seek transfer.
Technology moves readily; the question is whether it is shared.
Training is generally welcomed.

questions.stem: Why may the tax revenue benefit of an MNC be far smaller than expected?
options: Tax holidays and transfer pricing can mean little tax is paid locally
Multinationals are legally exempt from all taxation
Host governments are forbidden from taxing foreign firms
Corporation tax is collected only in the home country
questions.why: Governments competing for investment also bid each other's tax rates down, which is a race to the bottom.
whyNot: They are taxable; the issue is where profit is reported.
Host governments do tax foreign firms.
Tax is due where profit is deemed to arise.

questions.stem: What determines how much of an MNC's value creation stays in the host country?
options: Local sourcing, local employment at all levels, reinvested profit and tax actually paid
The size of the multinational's global revenue
The number of countries the multinational operates in
The exchange rate on the day of the investment
questions.why: An operation importing all its inputs and repatriating its profit creates jobs and little else.
whyNot: Global scale says nothing about local retention.
Geographic spread is not the relevant measure.
A single day's rate is not a structural factor.

questions.stem: Why does a small economy usually have weak bargaining power with an MNC?
options: It competes with other countries for the same investment, so it offers incentives instead of extracting conditions
Its laws do not apply to foreign companies
It cannot levy any taxes
Small economies are not permitted to negotiate
questions.why: A large economy with a skilled workforce and a market the MNC wants can negotiate on employment, sourcing and technology transfer.
whyNot: National law applies to operations within the country.
Small economies levy taxes normally.
They can negotiate; their leverage is simply weaker.

questions.stem: Which asymmetry explains why governments compete to attract FDI and are later disappointed?
options: Benefits such as jobs are immediate and visible, while costs are gradual and cumulative
Benefits are always overstated in official statistics
Costs are paid by the multinational rather than the country
Governments cannot measure either benefits or costs
questions.why: This asymmetry makes a strong concluding point in an essay on MNC impact.
whyNot: Both are measured with varying accuracy.
Environmental and social costs fall on the host country.
Both can be measured, at least partially.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a local environmental cost of an MNC's operation?
options: Emissions, waste, water use and pressure on land
The repatriation of profit to the home country
The use of transfer pricing to reduce tax
A rise in the host country's exchange rate
questions.why: Where regulation is weak, standards may be far below those the same company applies at home.
whyNot: That is a financial effect.
That is a fiscal effect.
That is a macroeconomic effect.

questions.stem: How can an MNC raise standards among local suppliers?
options: By requiring quality and reliability, which makes them more competitive generally
By buying all their output at the lowest possible price
By refusing to buy anything locally
By employing their staff directly
questions.why: The offsetting risk is that suppliers become dependent on one dominant customer with enormous bargaining power.
whyNot: Price pressure alone does not raise capability.
Not buying locally transfers nothing.
That removes suppliers rather than developing them.

questions.stem: In a small island tourism economy, what is the central question about MNC impact?
options: What share of the value created stays in the country
Whether the multinational brings any benefits at all
Whether tourists prefer local or foreign ownership
Whether the country should ban foreign investment
questions.why: High import content, profit repatriation and expatriate senior management all reduce the retained share, even though jobs and tax revenue are real.
whyNot: Benefits clearly exist; the question is their distribution.
Guest preference is not the economic issue.
A ban would forgo the benefits as well as the costs.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the multiplier effect?
options: An initial injection of spending generating further rounds of income and spending
The tendency of multinationals to have many subsidiaries
The growth of a market as incomes rise
The effect of advertising on total demand
questions.why: It is one of the mechanisms by which local incomes and national growth rise after an investment.
whyNot: That is corporate structure.
That is market growth.
That is a marketing effect.
